title: Yoga (revisited)
hook: two hikers, one trail map: Samkhya studies it, Yoga laces up its boots

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Samkhya Karika: the witness was never really bound, and the seer stands alone, kaivalya. When a feeling colored everything, could you let the color be the flower's? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

Two friends have the same trail map spread across a kitchen table. One of them traces every contour line, names every peak, learns where each stream comes from and where it goes. The other folds the map into a pocket and starts lacing up her boots. They aren't arguing. They're using the same map in two ways. For ten days we've been reading Samkhya's map: the seer, the seen, the strands, the count. Today we meet the darshana that took that map and laced up its boots. We've met it before on this path. Now we revisit it as a school: Yoga.
screen: `ONE MAP, TWO FRIENDS.` → `ONE STUDIES, ONE WALKS.` → `YOGA, AS A SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: The root text of the Yoga darshana is the Yoga Sutra, credited by tradition to Patanjali. Read it right after the Samkhya Karika and the furniture looks familiar. The Sutra speaks of the seer and the seen. It says the seen is made of the three gunas, light, activity and inertia, and of the elements and the senses. It says the seen exists for the seer's sake, for experience and for release. That's Samkhya's map, nearly line for line. But the Sutra asks a practical question: how do you get the confusion to clear? Its second verse answers: yoga is the stilling of the movements of the mind. And the next verse says what happens then. The seer rests in its own nature. That's the crystal from yesterday, with the red flower moved away. Then Yoga adds two things of its own. First, a whole program of practice: ethics, posture, breath, withdrawing the senses, concentration, meditation, absorption. Second, Ishvara, a special purusha untouched by affliction and karma, and the Sutra offers devotion to Ishvara as one path to stillness. The Samkhya Karika says nothing of Ishvara, and the schools are allowed to differ. And one verse speaks right to the dancer's bow. For the one whose seeing is complete, the Sutra says, the seen has ended, but it hasn't ended for everyone else, because it's shared. The dance goes on for the rest of the audience. So Yoga isn't stretching with a philosophy attached. It's Samkhya's map, walked.
screen: `THE SAME MAP: SEER AND SEEN.` · `STILLING THE MIND'S MOVEMENTS.` · `YOGA ADDS PRACTICE AND ISHVARA.` · `THE DANCE GOES ON FOR OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step on the map. Sit tall and comfortable, and let the breath slow. Then give the mind one thing to rest on, the feel of the breath at the nostrils. Each time the mind moves, to a plan, a sound, a memory, notice the movement and come back. You're not forcing anything still. You're just letting the movements settle, the way water clears when no one stirs it. If you pray, you can rest in Ishvara, or whatever you pray to, as the Sutra allows. The bell holds the time.
Yoga. As a darshana, the school of Patanjali's Yoga Sutra: Samkhya's map of seer and seen, walked through practice, with room for Ishvara.
Your line: Yoga, revisited. Today, once, when your mind is racing, give it one thing to rest on for three breaths, and watch the water clear a little. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Students of the Yoga darshana read Patanjali's Yoga Sutra with its classical commentary attributed to Vyasa, and practitioners in a number of lineages take up its eight limbs, from ethics and posture to meditation.

original.note: Sanskrit: in the Yoga Sutra, the stilling of the movements of the mind; also the name of the darshana.

trapdoor: what you thought: yoga is stretching with a philosophy attached.
what it means: a darshana that takes Samkhya's map of seer and seen and walks it, through practice and devotion to Ishvara.
what a scholar hears: Yoga Sutra 1.2–1.3 on citta-vritti-nirodha and the seer's rest, 1.24 on Ishvara, and 2.17–2.22 on seer, seen and the gunas.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 1.2–1.3 (yoga as stilling the mind's movements; the seer rests in its own nature)
Yoga Sutra 1.23–1.24 (devotion to Ishvara; Ishvara a special purusha untouched by affliction and karma)
Yoga Sutra 2.17–2.22 (seer and seen; the seen made of gunas, elements and senses, for experience and release; not ended for others)

notes: First day of the Yoga (revisited) week (1181–1186), opening a new week; it bridges from Samkhya (1171–1180) and is careful to present the two as one map used two ways, not ranked.
'For ten days we've been reading Samkhya's map' counts this path's own Samkhya days (1171–1180), not a fact about the texts.

Yoga Sutra paraphrases: 1.2 (yogash chitta-vritti-nirodhah), 1.3 (the seer abides in its own form), 1.23–24 (Ishvara-pranidhana; Ishvara as purusha-vishesha untouched by kleshas, karma, its fruits and residues), 2.18 (the seen: prakasha, kriya, sthiti; elements and senses; for bhoga and apavarga), 2.21 (the seen for the seer's sake), 2.22 (ended for one whose purpose is done, not for others, being common), 2.29 (the eight limbs). Confirm.
'The Samkhya Karika doesn't make room for that' (Ishvara): classical Samkhya as in the Karika does not posit Ishvara. Confirm the phrasing is fair and not a ranking.
